column2: Because he devours the lives of those who do harm, O greatly radiant one, one who desires his own well-being should give up meat.
Fierce destroyers of living beings find no protector; they are a terror to creatures, like beasts of prey.
Through greed, delusion of mind, or for strength and vigour, or through association with the wicked, men come to take pleasure in unrighteousness.
One who wishes to enlarge his own flesh with another's flesh is born, wherever he lives, in a dwelling of fear.
The restrained great sages say that not eating meat brings wealth, fame, long life, heaven and great blessing.
Now, son of Kunti, this I heard long ago from Markandeya, as he spoke of the faults in eating meat.
He who eats the flesh of living beings who desire to live, whether killed or dead, is just like the one who kills them.
One who buys with money kills; the eater kills by enjoyment; the slayer kills by killing and binding. Thus killing is of three kinds.
A man who neither eats nor consents, but approves "it should be killed" by a fault of intention, is also stained with the fault.
One who does not eat meat, compassionate to living beings here, becomes unassailable by all beings, long-lived, healthy and happy.
The tradition says that the dharma of not eating meat is better than gifts of gold, cows and land, in every way.
One should not eat meat that is unsprinkled, needless or against rule; a man who eats it goes to hell, without doubt.
Meat that is sprinkled and consecrated, and for a brahmin's wish, is to be known as of little fault here; otherwise one is stained.
The lowest of men who kills a creature for an eater's sake does great wrong; there the eater is at fault, not the killer.
The ignorant man who, greedy for meat, kills a creature by the ways laid down in sacrifice and the Vedic texts is surely a man destined for hell.
One who, having eaten meat, afterwards turns away, also has very great dharma, for he turns from sin.
The bringer, the approver, the cutter, the buyer and seller, the cook and the eater: all these are killers.
I shall tell you another authority, framed by rule, ancient, practised by sages and settled in the Vedas.
In the dharma marked by action, pursued by seekers of reward, it is as told, tiger among kings, but not for those who desire liberation.
The oblation consecrated with mantras, sprinkled and pure, by the Vedic authority and in the rites for the ancestors; otherwise, Manu said, meat is wasteful and not to be eaten.
It is not conducive to heaven, nor to fame, and is demonic, best of the Bharatas; in the old days men ate meat only by rule, O king.
A man who wishes for himself lasting freedom from trouble should avoid altogether the flesh of living beings here.
It is heard that in the earlier age the animal of men was made of rice, with which sacrificers intent on holy worlds sacrificed.
Asked a doubt by the sages, Vasu, lord of the Chedis, once said that meat was not to be eaten, and then that it was, O lord.
From the sky he fell to the earth, that lord of the earth; and having said this again, he entered the surface of the earth.
For the good of creatures, the great-souled Agastya consecrated by his austerity all forest beasts as sacred to all the gods.
In this way rites resting on the ancestors and gods are not lost, and the ancestors are justly pleased, gratified with meat.
But hear this, king of kings, as I tell it, blameless one: in not eating meat lies all happiness, O lord of men.
One who practises terrible austerity for a full hundred years, and one who gives up meat for one year, are equal in my view.
Especially in the Kaumuda bright fortnight, O lord of men, one should give up all meat, for dharma is enjoined there.
One who gives up meat for the four rainy months gains four blessings: fame, long life, glory and strength.
Or if for even one month one eats no meat of any kind, he passes beyond all sorrows and lives happy and healthy.
For those who give up meat by the month or by the fortnight, and are turned from harm, Brahma's world is ordained.
Meat in the Kaumuda fortnight has been avoided, Partha, by kings who were the self of all beings and knew the higher and lower.
By Nabhaga, Ambarisha, the great-souled Gaya, Ayus, Anaranya, Dilipa, Raghu and Puru,
by Kartavirya and Aniruddha, Nahusha and Yayati, Nriga, Vishvagashva, Shashabindu, Yuvanashva, and Shibi Aushinara,
by Shyenachitra, O king of kings, Somaka, Vrika, Raivata, Rantideva, Vasu and Srinjaya,
by Dushyanta, Karusha, Rama, Alarka and Nala, Virupashva, Nimi, and the wise Janaka,
by Sila and Prithu, by Virasena, Ikshvaku, Shambhu, Shveta and Sagara,
by these and others, O king of kings, meat was not eaten in the old days in the autumn Kaumuda month, and so they gained heaven.
They stay in Brahma's world, blazing and glorious, served by gandharvas and accompanied by thousands of women.
This supreme, auspicious dharma marked by non-harm: the great souls who practise it dwell on the back of heaven.
The righteous who here always give up honey and meat and, from birth, liquor, are all held to be sages, and attain pre-eminence among kinsmen, without doubt.
One in distress is freed from distress, a bound man from bonds, a sick man from sickness, and a sorrowing man from sorrow.
He does not go to an animal womb; he is handsome, wise, O best of the Kurus, and gains great fame.
This has been told to you, O king, on giving up meat, and the rule of engagement and withdrawal framed by the sages.
They do not so desire cakes of various forms, various vegetables, the shadava dishes and mixtures of flavours as they do meat.
On this my mind is bewildered at this point: I do not think there is anything here better in taste than meat.
So I wish to hear the merits of not eating meat, and the faults in eating it, O best of men.
Tell me all of it truly, knower of dharma, rightly and by dharma: what may be eaten and what may not.
[Bhishma] It is so, mighty-armed one, as you say, O Bharata: there is nothing else on earth that so exceeds meat in taste.
For those wasted by wounds and tormented, those given to worldly pleasures, and those worn by travel, there is nothing better than meat.
It at once increases the vital breaths and gives the best nourishment; no food exceeds meat, scourge of foes.
But in giving it up there are many merits, delight of the Kurus, that come to men; hear them as I tell them.
One who wishes to enlarge his own flesh with the flesh of others, no man is meaner than he or more cruel.
Nothing in the world is dearer than life; therefore a man should show compassion to others as to himself.
Meat arises, dear child, from semen, without doubt; and in eating it great fault comes together with the killing.
The knowers of the Veda know that dharma is marked by non-harm; what action is harmless, a self-possessed man should do.
In sacrifices to ancestors and gods the oblation is called consecrated; when eaten by the rule seen in the Veda, one is not stained.
It is also heard in scripture that animals were created for sacrifice; for those acting otherwise, the rule is called demonic.
Hear also from me the rule seen for kshatriyas, by which meat won by valour does not stain him who eats it.
The forest beasts were all consecrated as sacred to all the gods by Agastya long ago, O king, and so hunting is honoured.
There is no hunting without risking oneself; meeting on equal terms, one may slay the beast, or may not.
Therefore all royal sages go hunting, O Bharata; they are not stained by fault, and they do not hold it a sin.
For nothing is higher, here and hereafter, than compassion toward all beings in this world, delight of the Kurus.
A compassionate man never has fear here; these worlds and the next belong to the compassionate and to ascetics.
We have heard that beings give freedom from fear to him who, devoted to compassion, gives freedom from fear to all beings.
Wounded, stumbling, fallen, afflicted or struck, all beings protect him, on level and uneven ground.
Beasts of prey do not kill him, nor do pishachas or rakshasas; he is freed in times of fear, and frees others.
There is no gift higher than giving life, nor was, nor will be; it is certain that nothing is dearer to one than oneself.
Death is disagreeable to all beings, O Bharata; at the time of death trembling arises in them at once.
In the sorrows of birth, rebirth and old age, in the ocean of rebirth, creatures ever turn and shrink from death.
In the womb they are cooked by bitter, sour and pungent humours, and by the very cruel touch of urine, phlegm and faeces.
Born, helpless, they are torn again and again and shown cut open, helpless, those who craved meat.
They are cooked in the Kumbhi hell, reaching one womb after another; attacked and killed, they wander again and again.
Nothing on earth is dearer than oneself; therefore one should be compassionate and self-possessed toward all beings.
One who for all his life, O king, eats no meat of any kind attains a vast place in heaven, without doubt.
Those who eat the flesh of beings who wish to live are in turn eaten by those beings; of this I have no doubt.
He eats me, therefore I shall eat him: this is the meaning of the word for meat (mamsa); understand it, O Bharata.
The killer is always killed, and the binder bound; the reviler is reviled, O king, and the hater is hated.
By whatever body one does whatever deed, with that very body one enjoys its fruit.
Non-harm is the highest dharma, non-harm is the highest self-control, non-harm is the highest gift, non-harm is the highest austerity.
Non-harm is the highest sacrifice, non-harm is the highest strength, non-harm is the highest friend, non-harm the highest happiness, non-harm the highest truth, non-harm the highest teaching.
Gifts in all sacrifices, bathing in all tirthas, or the fruit of all gifts: none of this is equal to non-harm.
The austerity of the non-harming is inexhaustible; the non-harming always sacrifices; the non-harming is to all beings as mother and father.
This is the fruit of non-harm, and more, O best of the Kurus; its virtues cannot be told here even in hundreds of years.
[Yudhishthira] The giving up of life by men in a great battle is painful; I know the truth, knower of dharma, that giving up life is very hard.
Whether in prosperity or in adversity, in good or in ill, tell me the reason there, for you are held by me to be all-knowing.
[Bhishma] Whether in prosperity or in adversity, in good or in ill, beings born in this cycle of rebirth, O lord of the earth,
hear from me the reason by which feeling they are fond of life. This is a good question you have put, Yudhishthira.
On this I shall tell you, O king, an old event: the dialogue between Dvaipayana and an insect, Yudhishthira.
Once the brahmin Krishna Dvaipayana, moving as one with Brahman, saw an insect running swiftly on a cart-track.
Knowing the course of all beings and the cries of embodied creatures, all-knowing and all-giving, he saw the insect and spoke.
Insect, you seem terrified and hasty. Where do you run? Tell me, from where has this fear come to you?
[Bhishma] Thus addressed, he said to him: "Where is there happiness for you, insect? I think death would be happiness for you, since you live in an animal womb.
You do not know sound, touch, taste, smell and the many high and low enjoyments, insect; death is better for you."
[Insect] "The soul takes delight everywhere, and so here too I have happiness, great sage; I am aware of it, and therefore I wish to live.
Here too all objects are as the body prompts; humans and animals have separate enjoyments, specially.
In the past I was a man, a wealthy shudra, hostile to brahmins, cruel, a miser and a usurer.
Sharp of tongue, crafty of mind, a robber of everyone, secretly a destroyer, devoted to taking others' property.
In my house I kept servants and guests with stale food, from spite, a cruel man wanting good flavour and wishing to prosper.
Food prepared out of faith for gods and for ancestral sacrifice I did not give, desiring wealth; food that should be given purifies.
Those who came for refuge in times of fear, taking shelter in a hidden place, I abandoned, not out of sudden fear, and I did not protect the fearful.
Seeing men's wealth, grain, beloved wives, vehicles, clothes and marvellous prosperity, I was envious to no purpose.
Envious on seeing another's happiness, aggressive, wishing no one's prosperity, destroying others' three aims, following my own desire,
I remember the deeds I did long ago, full of cruel qualities, and I repent them, as one gives up a dear son.
I know too the fruit of my good deeds: I honoured my aged mother, and I honoured a brahmin.
Once a guest endowed with good birth and merit, having met me, came to my house, and I honoured him, O brahmin; by that my memory did not leave me.
By that deed I see hope of happiness here. I wish to hear from you what is best, wealthy in austerity."
[Vyasa] "By mere sight I help you across, by the power of austerity; and there is no other strength greater than the strength of austerity.
I know that you went to this state by your own sins, insect; you will gain the highest dharma if you, standing in dharma, think so.
The gods and the animals enjoy what is made in the field of action; and among men, by dharma, desire and wealth come according to merits.
What does a wise man lose, endowed with speech, mind, hands and feet, even if he lives dull-witted?
A living man performs the worship of the moon and the sun, foremost of brahmins; how, insect, will you come to holy worship there?
You will enjoy beings who are the qualities there; and there I shall lead you to Brahma-hood, wherever you wish."
Agreeing "So be it," the insect stayed on the road; he went to see that sage, through all the other wombs,
dog, iguana, boar, deer and birds, the wombs of the dog-eaters, vaishyas and shudras, and kshatriyas.
[Insect] "This is that incomparable place desired, with ten qualities, which I, having been an insect, have reached as a prince.
Very strong elephants with gold garlands carry me, and in chariots Kambojas, the finest horses, are yoked.
Vehicles yoked with camels and mules carry me; with my kin and ministers I eat meat and rice.
In well-appointed houses, on pleasant couches, and the most precious ones, O fortunate one, I sleep here well honoured.
In every last watch of the night, bards, heralds and panegyrists praise me with pleasing words as they do the god Mahendra.
By the favour of you whose word is true and splendour is boundless, I, who was an insect, have come to princehood.
Salutations to you, great sage; what shall I do? Command me. By the power of your austerity this has been shown to me."
[Vyasa] "I have been honoured by you today with words, O king, by chance. Today you, having been an insect, have recovered a memory free of disgust.
Yet there is no end of the sin you accumulated long ago as a shudra, intent on wealth, cruel and aggressive.
You have come to see me, and that was your earlier good deed, born in an animal womb, and also by your honouring me.
From this princehood you will reach brahmin-hood, having offered your life on the battlefield for cows and brahmins.
Having had the happiness of a prince and sacrifices with fees given, you will then rejoice in heaven, one with Brahman, imperishable and happy.
From an animal womb one goes to shudra-hood; a shudra to vaishya-hood and kshatriya-hood; a vaishya, a kshatriya praising good conduct, to brahmin-hood; a brahmin of good conduct to holy heaven."
Protect all subjects rightly, knowing good and ill, self-possessed, sharing out good things with desires and the cleansing of evil ones.
Be self-possessed and glad, intent on your own dharma; giving up the kshatriya body, you will then become a brahmin.
[Bhishma] Then, Yudhishthira, he went to the forest and, having heard the great sage's words and ruled his subjects by dharma,
in no long time that insect, best of kings, by the dharma of protecting subjects, died and became a brahmin.
Then, seeing that brahmin again, the greatly renowned and wise Krishna Dvaipayana came.
[Vyasa] "O best of brahmins, glorious one, do not be troubled in any way; the doer of good enters good wombs and the doer of evil evil wombs, O knower of dharma, according to dharma and tradition."
[Bhishma] On this too they cite an ancient tale: the dialogue between Maitreya and Krishna Dvaipayana.
Krishna Dvaipayana, O king, going about unrecognised, came to Maitreya in Varanasi, in a low woman's family.
Knowing him present and seated, the best of sages, Maitreya honoured him and fed him the finest food.
Having eaten that excellent, virtuous food, which satisfied every wish, the great-minded Krishna, as he departed, smiled, pleased.
Seeing him smile, Maitreya said to Krishna: "Tell me the reason, righteous one: why did you smile, and from what? Great joy has come to you, steadfast ascetic.
I ask you this, wise one, having bowed and saluted you, about your own austerity, fortune and good fortune.
Practising separately, dear friend, each of us for himself, I think the difference between us is small, or you are the more distinguished."
[Vyasa] "This time has come through excessive cutting and excessive talk; the Veda's word is untruth; why would the Veda speak what is false?
After happiness comes sorrow, and after sorrow happiness; this is seen, great sage, to be fixed by nature.
The wise say that a man's conduct here is of three kinds: one is merit, one is sin, and one is neither merit nor sin.
One does not think another's conduct good, and another's sin; so one's own deed completed is neither merit nor sin.
Enjoy, prosper, rejoice, give and sacrifice; neither physicians nor ascetics will overcome you."
[Vyasa] "Whatever you wish, Maitreya, as much as you wish, tell it, great sage; I wish to hear your words."
[Maitreya] "Your words, free of fault and stain, are joined with giving. By knowledge and austerity you are of cultivated soul, without doubt.
Because you are of cultivated soul, this gift to me is very great. I see more, by understanding, as if you were of abundant austerity.
Even by seeing you alone, great good has come to me. I think this is your favour; that deed is of your nature.
Austerity, learning and birth are the cause of brahminhood; one who is endowed with the three qualities becomes truly twice-born.
When he is satisfied, the ancestors and gods are satisfied; there is nothing greater for the learned than a brahmin.
As a man finds fruit in a well-tilled field, so the giver gets the fruit by giving to a learned man."
[Vyasa] "Beauty, pride, youth and pride of fortune do not, by good fortune, overcome you; this is the gods' favour for you. Hear what I shall tell you, that is greater than giving.
Whatever scriptures there are here, and whatever practices, they proceed in order with the Veda placed first.
I praise giving, and you too praise austerity and learning; austerity is the Veda's purifier, and austerity is the means to heaven.
We have heard that by austerity one gains greatness and by knowledge; and by austerity alone one may remove any other evil deed.
Whatever a man, setting his mind on something, practises austerity for, a brahmin who has mastered the Veda obtains all that.
What is hard to follow, hard to assail, hard to gain, hard to cross, all that austerity overcomes; austerity is indeed stronger.
A drinker of liquor, one who takes what is not allowed, a killer of embryos, one who defiles his teacher's bed, crosses over all by austerity and is freed from sin.
One who knows all knowledge and one who has sight, whatever their kind, are called the two ascetics; salutations should always be made to them."

By what conduct, auspicious one, or what way of life did you shake off all sins and come to the world of the gods?

mahabharata:13:124.6	You have not come to this world by little austerity, gift or observance; therefore tell me the truth.

mahabharata:13:124.15	Whatever work was brought for the household I rose in the morning and had it all done and did it.

[Bhishma] Some are appeased by conciliation and another by gift; knowing a man's nature, one should choose one of the two.
Hear from me, O king, the merits of conciliation, O best of the Bharatas, how even fierce beings may be propitiated by it.
On this too they cite an ancient tale, how a twice-born seized by a rakshasa in a forest was freed.
A brahmin endowed with wisdom, in a lonely forest, was seized and brought into distress by a rakshasa who meant to eat him.
Endowed with wisdom and learning, seeing that very terrible being, he used only conciliation on him; he was not bewildered and not shaken.
The rakshasa, honouring him with words, put a question to the twice-born: "You will be freed; tell me this: why am I pale and lean?"
After thinking a moment, the brahmin, unflustered, answered the rakshasa's question with these verses.

You are living abroad, in a strange land, surely without your friends, enjoying incomparable pleasures; so you are pale and lean.

mahabharata:13:125.14	Having pressed yourself down out of nobility, you have favoured someone, good one, who thinks he has defeated you; so you are pale and lean.
